The skill tells a story.

tweets.text:
@kurtextrem
 had a great idea: give agents a space to list implicit decisions in the PR template.

The skill makes them first-class citizens with their own UI.

Most of the feedback I end up giving is related to these.

tweets.name: Pablo Caballero 🦀
tweets.text:
Not only do I use the skill to parse AI output or PRs assigned to me. I also use them to make walkthroughs for my own PRs.

I write my own words, structure sections as I want, and send my colleagues the summary instead of the PR.

They review exactly what I need reviewed.

Now, are humans still relevant at all when reviewing code?

Opus 5.5 marked an inflection point: I now feel comfortable giving up control over part of the code.

But unless you're making an MVP, I believe our input is still necessary on high-level decisions.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
Nov 1-16 already beat all of October (18,269). Over 16 months that's 53.3K clicks and 4M impressions, with 0 paid ads.

And this is how traffic grows when you don't let AI do your entire SEO.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
1. Take the exact search people type and make it your homepage H1 and title. Then turn your H2s into the questions they ask and add an FAQ, dead simple.

Ours went from 10 to 17 questions.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
2. Fix the basics before you write anything new. Crawl your own site and make sure every page has one H1, menus are real links (not JavaScript buttons) and pages are prerendered.

One of ours had 11 H1s, and response time dropped from 0.5s+ to 0.1-0.2s.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
3. Kill your duplicate pages. Find pages sharing a title or description, give each its own URL, title and description, then redirect the old URLs.

We had 22 product pages sharing ONE title, which is just sad.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
4. Give every comparison search its own page. Write the spec first (sections, FAQs, internal links, a verdict), then build every page to it so none ends up thin.

We built 136 pages to one spec: 8 sections, 6 FAQs, 8+ internal links.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
5. Build hubs. Group related pages under a hub with a guide section and an FAQ, and show related posts under every blog post so no page sits on its own.

We built 16 hubs at 1,500-1,900 words each.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
6. Publish data nobody else has. Use what only you have, like your users' results, your own numbers, your own tool. If Google can get it elsewhere, why would it rank you?

Ours is a tool with live averages from our own users, and nobody can copy that.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
7. Translate what already works. Check Search Console for countries already showing impressions, translate your proven pages for them, add hreflang, then actually review the translations.

We run 15 languages and one review pass fixed about 1,800 strings.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
8. Keep the blog going. Get real people to write it, on a schedule, at a pace you can keep for a year and not just a week.

Ours ran on a schedule the whole time, so stop overthinking it and just keep publishing.

tweets.name: Noel Ceta
tweets.text:
So where does AI fit? Let it type: the code, drafts to your spec, translations, and a check of every page against that spec.

You decide which searches matter, which page answers each, the spec, and what never ships (made-up stats, for one).

Don't let AI decide. Let it type.

Ran this on my e-signature app (SignuDoc fork). In 13 PRs:

Deleted ~470 comments and added a CI lint so new ones fail the build. A "why" note is allowed only with a ticket number.

Wrote 4 TLA+ models (deletion notices, download/audit, DB lock order, PDF render pool). They run in CI and replay real past bugs, which they catch.

The models found 3 real bugs in our deletion-notice emails and 2 database deadlocks. Every one was reproduced on real Postgres before it was fixed, and all of them have shipped.

Deleted 10,189 lines of implementation-pinning unit tests (47 files). Kept the 36 that guard security and legal behavior.

Turned on strict TypeScript flags and banned any and !. Added a "type ratchet" so unsafe casts can only go down.

Gave every ID and token its own type, so passing a signer ID where an envelope ID belongs, or a raw token where its hash belongs, no longer compiles.

Database rows are now parsed when they're loaded, not cast. That surfaced a type that had been lying about which columns a query returned.

Added a CI color-contrast check and a "verify your change" table in AGENTS.md, so agents know which check to run for each kind of change.

Nice I use something similar after watching this. 

Use $poteto-mode on this repository. Find recurring mistakes in its actual history, then remove the conditions that permit them. Deliver one verifiable PR per step and get its required CI checks green.

Start with evidence
- Read the repository instructions and applicable skills.
- Inspect git history, original bug-fix diffs, review comments, and failed CI evidence. Trace fixes back to the broken revisions and affected callers.
- Group incidents by shared root cause. For each group, record the source links or SHAs, observable failure, violated invariant, prior repair, and evidence of recurrence. Distinguish confirmed causes from hypotheses.
- Rank the groups by demonstrated harm and recurrence. Start with the smallest change that eliminates a proven class of mistakes. Do not manufacture findings to justify a sweep.

Choose the strongest practical constraint
For each selected group, try these in order:
1. Architecture that removes the invalid operation or shared mutable state.
2. Domain types and boundary validation that prevent invalid states.
3. A narrowly scoped lint whose error explains the concrete fix.
4. A behavioral test when the earlier options cannot enforce the constraint.

Explain why weaker layers remain necessary. Preserve required public compatibility. Prototype alternatives whenever an experiment can settle the choice, state the decision criterion first, and recommend the option supported by the observations. Leave genuine product or preference choices to me.

Prove the constraint
Before trusting any new enforcement, demonstrate that it catches the actual historical mistake:
- Replay the relevant broken revision, or introduce a faithful mutation of that defect when direct replay is impractical.
- Show failure for the intended invariant, then success with the correction.
- Check representative valid behavior so a rule that rejects everything cannot pass.
- Keep exact commands, revisions, failure output, and reproducible evidence with the PR.

Comments
Apply $no-comments

Scope this work to each selected change. Delete comments that restate code. Encode meaningful constraints in structure, types, validation, lint, or tests before removing their explanation. This request authorizes those encodings within scope. Preserve required legal notices and mandated public documentation. Report constraints that remain unenforced.

Formal verification
Where historical evidence identifies concurrency, retry, or state-machine defects, invoke /create-formal-verification-skill. Locate and read it first; report if it is unavailable rather than claiming to have used it.

Model the actual actors, state, transitions, failures, and environmental assumptions. State the safety properties and any relevant liveness properties separately. Reproduce the historical defect as a counterexample, correct the model, and run the checker in CI with explicit exploration bounds.

Map model transitions to production operations. Add concrete trace replay or real integration tests so an accurate model of inaccurate code cannot establish success. State what the model does and does not prove.

Tests
Replace implementation-pinning unit tests only after identifying their protected behavior and demonstrating replacement coverage through the model, real database tests, or end-to-end tests. Retain useful behavioral unit tests. Keep every test that guards security or legal behavior. Do not weaken gates or use skipped work as evidence of success.

Delivery
Use <task-slug> branches and one independently reviewable PR per step. Record dependencies between PRs. Follow the repository’s package-manager, formatting, service, and verification rules.

For each PR, include the historical evidence, invariant, chosen enforcement, red/green demonstration, runtime verification, and remaining limits. Run the required checks and resolve CI failures until green. PR delivery is the endpoint; merging and deployment require separate authorization.

Continue through the evidence-backed findings. Maintain a short decision log and report genuine access or capability blockers. Do not claim repository-wide prevention or formal correctness beyond the behavior and state space actually checked.
